{{Short description|Method of deducing if a new experiment gives more information than pre-existing ones}}
'''Incremental validity''' is a type of [[validity (statistics)|statistical validity]] that assesses whether a new [[psychometric]] assessment has more predictive ability than existing methods of assessment.<ref name="Sackett">{{cite journal|doi=10.1146/annurev.psych.59.103006.093716|title=Personnel Selection|year=2008|last1=Sackett|first1=Paul R.|last2=Lievens|first2=Filip|journal=[[Annual Review of Psychology]]|volume=59|pages=419–450|pmid=17854285|s2cid=44560725 }}</ref> It seeks to determine whether the new assessment adds information that cannot be obtained with simpler, already existing methods.<ref>Lillenfield et al. 2005 "What's wrong with this picture?" ''www.psychologicalscience.org'' http://www.psychologicalscience.org/newsresearch/publications/journals/sa1_2.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101224025816/http://www.psychologicalscience.org/newsresearch/publications/journals/sa1_2.pdf |date=2010-12-24 }}</ref>

New psychometric instruments are often assessed on whether it can increase knowledge of an outcome variable beyond what is already known based on existing instruments.<ref name="Haynes"> {{cite journal |last1=Haynes |first1=S.N. |last2=Lench |first2=H.C. |date=2003 |title=Incremental Validity of New Clinical Assessment Measures |url=http://heatherlench.com/wp-content/uploads/2006/08/incremental-validity.pdf |journal=Psychological Assessment |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=456–466 |doi=10.1037/1040-3590.15.4.456 |pmid=14692842 |access-date=13 December 2013}}</ref> If the instrument is less successful than an existing tool, then it is incrementally invalid.

Incremental validity is usually assessed using [[Linear_regression|multiple regression]] methods, involving a regression model with other variables fitted to the data and another model with the focal variable added. Using an [[F-test]] to determine [[Statistical significance|significance]], a significant difference in the [[R-square]] statistic reflects the percent of variance explained by the added variable, indicating whether that variable offers significant additional predictive power for the dependent variable over other variables. Using the change in R-square is more appropriate than mere raw correlations, because the raw correlations do not reflect the overlap of the newly introduced measure and the existing measures.<ref name="Haynes" />

For example, the [[College Board]] has used multiple regression models to assess the incremental validity of a revised SAT test.<ref name="Bridgeman">{{cite journal |last1=Bridgeman |first1=B. |last2=McCamley-Jenkins |first2=L. |last3=Ervin |first3=N. |date=2000 |title=Predictions of Freshman Grade-Point Average From the Revised and Recentered SAT® I: Reasoning Test |url=http://research.collegeboard.org/sites/default/files/publications/2012/7/researchreport-2000-1-predictions-freshman-gpa-revised-recentered-sat-reasoning.pdf |journal=Ets Rr 00-1 |publisher=Educational Testing Service, Princeton, NJ |access-date=13 December 2013 |archive-date=13 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131213222727/http://research.collegeboard.org/sites/default/files/publications/2012/7/researchreport-2000-1-predictions-freshman-gpa-revised-recentered-sat-reasoning.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>
